sections.heading: What are the symptoms of pneumonia?
sections.body:
The NHS says pneumonia symptoms can come on suddenly or build up over a few days. A cough, breathlessness and a fever are typical, and chest pain and confusion can also occur, with confusion being common in older people. Some people cough up yellow or green phlegm. Where the lining around the lung is also inflamed (pleurisy), the chest pain can be sharp and get worse when breathing.

The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for a cough that lasts about three weeks or more, yellow or green phlegm or breathlessness. It advises calling 999 for severe difficulty breathing, pale, blue or blotchy skin, lips or tongue, sudden confusion or coughing up more than streaks of blood, and says not to drive yourself to A&E. Pneumonia is more common, and can be more serious, in young children.

sections.heading: What causes pneumonia, and what are the complications?
sections.body:
Pneumonia is an infection of one or both lungs. Bacteria, viruses or fungi can cause it. The pneumococcus bacterium can cause pneumonia, and the vaccine against it is described below.

Aspiration, which means food or liquid going down into the lungs by mistake, can also cause pneumonia.

Pneumonia can affect people of any age. Pneumonia can be more serious in young children, in people over 65 and in people with other serious health problems, who are more likely to need hospital care.

Complications of pneumonia can include pleurisy, fluid around the lungs, a lung abscess, sepsis and respiratory failure.

sections.heading: How is pneumonia diagnosed?
sections.body:
NHS hospital leaflets describe a doctor first asking about symptoms and examining the chest. A chest X-ray may be arranged to confirm the diagnosis, and blood tests and tests on a sample of phlegm (sputum) may also be done.

Doctors often use a scoring system to gauge how serious the pneumonia is. NHS inform describes a scoring system called CRB-65 that estimates the risk of complications and whether urgent hospital treatment is needed. Most people recover at home, while people who are very unwell or at higher risk may be admitted.

In hospital the team can give antibiotics through a drip, and sometimes steroids, and may add oxygen to help breathing. The NHS says a follow-up chest X-ray is not routine for everyone. It may be arranged about six weeks later for some people, for example those who smoke or are over 50.

sections.heading: How is pneumonia treated, and how long does recovery take?
sections.body:
The NHS says antibiotics are the usual treatment when bacteria are the likely cause. Mild cases can often be treated at home with antibiotics, plenty of rest and plenty of fluids. Pneumonia caused by a virus does not need antibiotics.

People who are very unwell, or at higher risk, may be treated in hospital. There the usual treatment is antibiotics, often given into a vein, and sometimes steroids. Oxygen can be added to help with breathing.

Recovery varies from person to person. NHS guidance sets out a rough timeline: the high temperature should have gone after about a week, chest pain and mucus should have reduced substantially after about four weeks, and cough and breathlessness should have eased substantially after about six weeks. Most symptoms should have resolved by three months, although tiredness can linger, and most people feel back to normal by about six months.

Recovery can take longer in older people and in people with other health problems. The cough may last for two to three weeks after the antibiotics are finished, and tiredness can last longer as the body recovers. People who have had pneumonia are also more prone to other chest infections for a while.

sections.heading: Can pneumonia be prevented?
sections.body:
The pneumococcal vaccine helps protect against serious illnesses such as pneumonia, but it does not protect against illnesses caused by other bacteria or viruses. The pneumococcal vaccine helps protect against serious pneumococcal infections, which can lead to pneumonia, septicaemia and meningitis.

In the UK the pneumococcal vaccine is offered to babies as part of the routine childhood programme. The pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine is given to people aged 65 and over and to people at high risk because of long-term health conditions. The NHS also offers flu, RSV and COVID-19 vaccines to some groups, such as older people and people with certain long-term health conditions.

faqs.q: Do all cases of pneumonia need antibiotics?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says antibiotics are the usual treatment when bacteria are the likely cause, but pneumonia caused by a virus does not need antibiotics.

faqs.q: Can pneumonia be treated at home?
faqs.a: Mild cases can often be treated at home with antibiotics, rest and plenty of fluids. People who are very unwell, or at higher risk, may be treated in hospital, where antibiotics are often given into a vein and oxygen can be added.

faqs.q: Why does the cough last so long after pneumonia?
faqs.a: The NHS and hospital leaflets say a cough can carry on for two to three weeks after antibiotics are finished, and tiredness can last longer. NHS guidance sets out a rough timeline in which cough and breathlessness should have eased substantially after about six weeks.

faqs.q: When is pneumonia an emergency?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 for severe difficulty breathing, pale, blue or blotchy skin, lips or tongue, sudden confusion or coughing up more than streaks of blood, and not to drive yourself to A&E. For a cough that lasts about three weeks or more, yellow or green phlegm or breathlessness it advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine against pneumonia?
faqs.a: There are vaccines against some causes. The pneumococcal vaccine is offered to babies and to people aged 65 and over or at higher risk. Flu, RSV and COVID-19 vaccines are also advised for specific groups, but vaccines do not cover every cause of pneumonia.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of a heart attack?
sections.body:
The NHS says to call 999 for chest pain that feels tight or squeezing or that spreads to the arms, neck or jaw; other symptoms can include shortness of breath, feeling or being sick, sweating, and pale, blue or grey skin. A heart attack is a medical emergency.

Not everyone has the classic chest pain. NHS 111 Wales notes that women are more likely to have other symptoms such as shortness of breath, feeling or being sick, and back or jaw pain. Symptoms vary from person to person, and some people, including older adults and people with diabetes, may have milder or atypical symptoms.

The NHS advises that, while waiting for the ambulance, a person who is not allergic to aspirin may chew and swallow an aspirin tablet.

sections.heading: What causes a heart attack?
sections.body:
The NHS says a heart attack happens when the blood supply to part of the heart is suddenly cut off, so that the heart muscle begins to die. Coronary heart disease is the leading cause. In coronary heart disease, fatty plaques build up in the coronary arteries, and a plaque can rupture and trigger a clot that blocks the vessel. A shortage of oxygen in the blood, for example from carbon monoxide poisoning or lung problems, is a less common cause.

The NHS lists smoking, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, being overweight and a close relative who has had a heart attack among the risk factors. NHS Inform lists age and ethnicity among the risk factors for coronary heart disease.

A heart attack is a problem with the blood supply to the heart muscle. Cardiac arrest is different: the NHS says that if a large part of the heart is damaged, the heart can stop beating altogether.

sections.heading: How is a heart attack diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says the main tests for finding out whether someone is having a heart attack are an electrocardiogram (ECG) and blood tests.

There are two main types. In a STEMI, the ECG shows a rise in a part of the tracing called the ST segment. In an NSTEMI, the ECG does not show the ST rise seen in a STEMI, and it can look normal or show other changes.

Troponin, a marker of damage to the heart muscle, is measured in blood tests. Troponin is the preferred blood marker for diagnosing a heart attack, and a raised level with an ECG that lacks STEMI changes points to an NSTEMI. A BHF-funded trial in Edinburgh found that a high-sensitivity troponin test doubled the number of women diagnosed with a heart attack.

sections.heading: How is a heart attack treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says the choice of treatment depends on how severe the heart attack is. The NHS lists medicines to treat the blockage, angioplasty with a stent, and coronary artery bypass surgery. In angioplasty, a small plastic tube called a stent is used to open a blocked artery.

For a STEMI, the usual approach is to offer a coronary angiogram, which images the arteries, followed by primary percutaneous coronary intervention (primary PCI), meaning emergency angioplasty, when symptoms began recently enough for it to help. NICE guideline NG185 covers the early management of acute coronary syndromes.

The BHF says most people stay in hospital for about two to five days after a heart attack, and for two or three days after coronary angioplasty or stents.

 The NHS describes rupture of the heart's muscle, walls or valves as an extremely serious but relatively uncommon complication of a heart attack.

sections.heading: What happens after a heart attack?
sections.body:
People are commonly prescribed medicines after a heart attack, such as antiplatelets, beta blockers and statins, to lower the chance of another one. The BHF says antiplatelet drugs such as clopidogrel or ticagrelor are commonly prescribed for a year, and most people are prescribed aspirin for life. Beta blockers and statins are also common, and a glyceryl trinitrate spray can ease chest pain.

The NHS says people are offered cardiac rehabilitation, which can be done in person or remotely. The BHF says cardiac rehabilitation usually starts around a month to six weeks after getting home from hospital, and typically covers topics such as driving, returning to work and holidays.

The NHS says recovery after a heart attack can take several weeks or longer, and hospital guidance says when someone can return to work depends on their job, how severe the heart attack was and how quickly they recover. A GP can provide a fit note if someone is not fit for work.

sections.heading: Feelings, anxiety and sex after a heart attack
sections.body:
The BHF says rehabilitation should include support for wellbeing, including an assessment of anxiety or depression, tips for dealing with stress and information on other sources of help.

Most people can return to having sex after a heart attack, and NHS 111 Wales, citing the BHF, gives about four to six weeks as a usual time.

 Chest pain that feels tight or squeezing, or that spreads to the arms, neck or jaw, is a reason to call 999 immediately, as described at the top of this article.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a heart attack and cardiac arrest?
faqs.a: In a heart attack the blood supply to part of the heart muscle is suddenly cut off. In cardiac arrest the heart stops beating. The NHS says that if a large part of the heart is damaged in a heart attack, the heart can stop beating altogether.

faqs.q: Do women have different heart attack symptoms?
faqs.a: NHS 111 Wales notes women are more likely to have other symptoms too, such as breathlessness, feeling sick, and back or jaw pain.

faqs.q: How long do people stay in hospital?
faqs.a: The BHF says people usually stay in hospital for about two to five days after a heart attack. If they have had coronary angioplasty or stents, the stay is likely to be 2 or 3 days.

faqs.q: Will I need heart medicines for life?
faqs.a: The BHF says antiplatelets such as clopidogrel or ticagrelor are commonly prescribed for a year, and most people are prescribed aspirin for life. Beta blockers and statins are also common.

faqs.q: When can I have sex again after a heart attack?
faqs.a: Most people can return to having sex after a heart attack, and NHS 111 Wales, citing the BHF, gives about four to six weeks as a usual time.

sections.heading: How is a DVT assessed in practice?
sections.body:
NICE says that people with a likely DVT should have a leg vein ultrasound scan within 4 hours of it being requested, or within 24 hours if that is not possible.

NHS inform says that if a doctor thinks you have DVT, you will need tests, including a blood test called a D-dimer and/or an ultrasound scan. The doctor first estimates the likelihood of a clot using a points score called the Wells score. In NHS guidance, people with a low Wells score but a positive D-dimer test are recommended to have an ultrasound scan. If the Wells score shows that a DVT is likely, NICE says the person should have a leg vein ultrasound scan.

DVT can occur in an arm as well as a leg. Typical symptoms include throbbing pain, usually in the calf or thigh, and swelling in one leg, often with swollen veins, although a clot can sometimes cause no symptoms. The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if leg symptoms come with breathlessness or chest pain.

sections.heading: How is a DVT treated?
sections.body:
Blood-thinning medicines (anticoagulants) are the main treatment. NHS hospital leaflets describe treatment with blood-thinning tablets such as rivaroxaban or apixaban, or with warfarin or heparin injections. The NHS says people usually need to take them for at least three months to reduce the risk of another clot.

 NHS hospital leaflets say that if it is not a first DVT, treatment is normally recommended for life.

Anticoagulants reduce the risk of the clot getting worse and give the body time to break the clot down. The body breaks the clot down over time. The medicine stops the clot growing and reduces the risk of another clot. Clot-busting drugs or surgery are reserved for severe cases.

sections.heading: Living with blood thinners
sections.body:
NHS hospital leaflets list minor bruising or bleeding as the most common side effect of blood-thinning injections such as dalteparin. NHS hospital leaflets list warning signs of bleeding on blood thinners, including blood when vomiting or coughing, black or bloody stools, blood in the urine, prolonged nosebleeds and unexplained or severe bruising, and advise seeking medical advice.

 NHS hospital leaflets say that combined contraceptive pills and HRT containing oestrogen can increase the risk of a DVT or pulmonary embolism.

 Some NHS hospital leaflets say aspirin has not been proven to reduce the risk of clots on long journeys.

sections.heading: What are the long-term effects of a DVT?
sections.body:
The most serious complication is a pulmonary embolism, in which a clot travels to the lungs. It can be life-threatening and needs to be treated quickly.

Post-thrombotic syndrome is a common long-term complication of DVT in the leg. A UCLH leaflet describes post-thrombotic syndrome as causing symptoms that include leg swelling, varicose veins and occasionally leg ulcers. Post-thrombotic syndrome usually appears within about six months to two years of the clot. Estimates of how many people develop post-thrombotic syndrome vary: a UCLH leaflet says 20 to 50 in 100, usually after extensive clots, while another hospital leaflet says about 1 in 4.

A UCLH leaflet says compression stockings may help with these symptoms. A UCLH leaflet says compression stockings should not be worn until the initial leg swelling has settled.

An NHS hospital leaflet advises regular exercise, with walking especially helpful, and regular short walking breaks on long journeys.

sections.heading: Who is at risk of a DVT, and what about pregnancy?
sections.body:
The NHS lists risk factors for DVT including being over 60, obesity, smoking, hormonal contraception or HRT, cancer and a previous DVT. The NHS also lists smoking, being over 60 and taking hormone replacement therapy as risk factors.

 NHS trust guidance says warfarin should not be used in pregnancy and that there is too little research on the newer oral anticoagulants in pregnancy. NHS trust guidance describes low-molecular-weight heparin injections as the usual choice for treating a clot in pregnancy.

faqs.q: Does a blood thinner dissolve the clot?
faqs.a: No. A hospital leaflet says anticoagulants reduce the risk of the clot getting worse and let the body break it down. The medicine stops the clot growing and reduces the risk of another clot. Clot-busting drugs or surgery are kept for severe cases.

faqs.q: How long are blood thinners taken for?
faqs.a: The NHS says people usually need them for at least three months. NHS hospital leaflets say that if it is not a first DVT, treatment is normally recommended for life. People prescribed a blood thinner are advised not to stop it without talking to a doctor.

faqs.q: When does a DVT become an emergency?
faqs.a: The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if leg symptoms come with breathlessness or chest pain, as this can mean the clot has reached the lungs. If a doctor thinks a leg clot is likely, NICE says an ultrasound scan should be available within 4 hours of it being requested, or within 24 hours if that is not possible.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of a pulmonary embolism?
sections.body:
The NHS lists sudden breathlessness, chest pain that gets worse when breathing in and coughing up blood as the main symptoms, with leg pain or swelling also possible if a DVT is present. The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E for sudden difficulty breathing, chest or upper back pain, a very fast heartbeat or passing out.

 Hospital leaflets note that a small pulmonary embolism may cause no symptoms at all. NICE guidance on suspected pulmonary embolism describes using a clinical probability score, followed by tests such as a D-dimer blood test or a scan.

sections.heading: What causes a pulmonary embolism?
sections.body:
NHS hospital leaflets say the clot is usually a deep vein thrombosis (DVT), most often in the leg or pelvis, that has travelled to the lungs. A few come from an arm vein or from a clot in the heart.

 Risk factors include pregnancy and the weeks after birth, oestrogen-containing contraception or hormone replacement therapy, and cancer. Some people have an inherited tendency for their blood to clot (thrombophilia), such as factor V Leiden.

Sometimes a pulmonary embolism happens for no obvious reason. Doctors describe these as unprovoked, and the likely cause is important in deciding how long treatment continues.

sections.heading: How is a pulmonary embolism diagnosed?
sections.body:
NICE guidance describes estimating the clinical probability of pulmonary embolism with a score, then using a D-dimer blood test or imaging depending on the result. A Whittington Health policy says a negative D-dimer test reliably excludes pulmonary embolism in people with a low clinical probability, so further imaging is not needed in that group.

The usual confirming scan is a CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA).

NICE guidance says that when a scan cannot be done straight away, people thought likely to have a pulmonary embolism are offered interim anticoagulant treatment until it can be done. Treatment can therefore begin before the scan result is back.

sections.heading: How is a pulmonary embolism treated?
sections.body:
Once the diagnosis is confirmed, treatment usually continues with anticoagulant tablets or injections, depending on what suits the person. Anticoagulants do not dissolve the clot. The body clears it over time. They stop existing clots growing and help prevent new ones forming. Clot-busting drugs (thrombolysis) are considered for people whose circulation is affected by a severe pulmonary embolism.

Hospital leaflets say treatment can last anywhere from three months to the rest of a person's life, depending on the cause and the person's risk of another clot.

Anticoagulants raise the risk of bleeding. Hospital leaflets list black or bloody stools, vomiting or coughing up blood, and heavy bleeding that does not stop as reasons to get urgent medical help, by calling NHS 111 or going to A&E.

sections.heading: What is recovery from a pulmonary embolism like?
sections.body:
The NHS says a full recovery is expected if a pulmonary embolism is spotted and treated early. Hospital leaflets say it is common to feel breathless for a few weeks or months after a pulmonary embolism. Hospital leaflets advise talking to a GP if breathlessness does not improve, and note that a minority of people have symptoms for a prolonged period.

Some people have longer-term problems. One NHS leaflet notes that a minority of people continue to have symptoms for a long time, which may be due to a condition called chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH).

 Questions about long-term treatment, travel or hormone medicines belong with the treating team or GP.

faqs.q: Where do the clots in a pulmonary embolism come from?
faqs.a: NHS hospital leaflets say the clot is usually a deep vein thrombosis (DVT), most often in the leg or pelvis, that has travelled to the lungs. A few come from an arm vein or from the heart.

faqs.q: Can a pulmonary embolism cause no symptoms?
faqs.a: Yes. Hospital leaflets note that a small pulmonary embolism may cause no symptoms at all. NICE guidance describes using a clinical probability score and tests such as a D-dimer blood test and a scan to diagnose it.

faqs.q: Why is a D-dimer test not enough on its own?
faqs.a: A negative D-dimer test reliably excludes pulmonary embolism in people with a low clinical probability, according to a Whittington Health policy. NICE guidance recommends imaging, usually a CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA), when a pulmonary embolism is thought likely.

faqs.q: How long does treatment last?
faqs.a: Hospital leaflets say it can last from three months to the rest of a person's life. The length depends on the cause of the clot and the risk of another one, and the treating team makes the decision.

faqs.q: How long does recovery take?
faqs.a: Hospital leaflets say it is common to feel breathless for a few weeks or months after a pulmonary embolism. The NHS says people should make a full recovery if the condition is spotted and treated early, though hospital leaflets say it is common to feel breathless for a few weeks or months.

sections.heading: What causes type 1 diabetes?
sections.body:
Type 1 diabetes is a lifelong condition in which the pancreas produces little or no insulin. It is an autoimmune condition: the immune system damages the insulin-producing cells of the pancreas.

Type 1 diabetes can run in families, but Diabetes UK says most people with type 1 have no family history of it. Diabetes UK says the exact cause of type 1 diabetes is not known, and that things in the environment, such as viruses, may play a part in triggering it.

In the UK, Diabetes UK reports that about 90% of people diagnosed with diabetes have type 2 and about 8% have type 1. The NHS lists the classic early signs as needing the toilet more, being thirsty, feeling tired and losing weight, often remembered as the four Ts. NIDDK notes that some people first find out they have type 1 diabetes when they develop signs of diabetic ketoacidosis.

sections.heading: How is type 1 diabetes diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP will usually test a urine sample and may check blood glucose, then send the person to hospital for assessment. The NHS says people are usually kept in hospital until their blood test results are back.

NIDDK says symptoms of type 1 diabetes usually develop quickly, over a few days or weeks. The other signs it lists are blurred vision, sweet or fruity-smelling breath, slow-healing cuts and frequent infections.

Because diabetic ketoacidosis can be the first sign, the NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if symptoms worsen quickly, or if stomach pain, sleepiness or confusion, or fast, deep breathing develop. The NHS advises seeing a GP about these symptoms, and calling 999 or going to A&E if they get worse quickly.

sections.heading: How is type 1 diabetes treated day to day?
sections.body:
The NHS says people with type 1 diabetes take insulin, either with pens or with a pump. Most people take both a long-acting insulin, once or twice a day, and a rapid-acting insulin before meals. This pattern is known as basal-bolus treatment.

Insulin can be given with pens or by a pump, which gives small amounts of rapid-acting insulin throughout the day. Pump therapy can be used by adults, teenagers and children with adult supervision.

The NHS says the dose of rapid-acting insulin at a meal is worked out from the amount of carbohydrate to be eaten, which is called carbohydrate counting.

One NHS 111 Wales page stresses that treatment should not be stopped during illness, and that the treatment plan may say whether a temporary increase is needed.

sections.heading: What is a hypo?
sections.body:
A hypo is a lower-than-normal level of glucose in the blood. The NHS lists feeling hungry, dizzy, sweaty and shaky among the signs of a hypo, and says that if it is not treated it can lead to drowsiness or loss of consciousness.

 Common triggers include too much insulin, a skipped meal, vigorous exercise and drinking alcohol on an empty stomach.

Mild hypos are usually treated with something sugary. In a severe hypo a person may become drowsy, confused or lose consciousness and may need a glucagon injection into a muscle or glucose given into a vein; the NHS says to call 999 and ask for an ambulance if they do not come round within 10 minutes of a glucagon injection.

NICE says the annual review should check that the person can recognise the symptoms of a hypo.

sections.heading: What is diabetic ketoacidosis?
sections.body:
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a medical emergency that can follow untreated type 1 diabetes and is treated in hospital with insulin and fluids. Diabetes UK lists being very thirsty, needing to wee more often, feeling tired and sleepy, confusion, blurred vision, stomach pain, feeling or being sick, and sweet or fruity-smelling breath; the NHS also lists breathing more deeply than usual. Diabetes UK and the NHS say DKA symptoms usually develop over about 24 hours but can come on faster.

The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if the symptoms are getting worse quickly, or if there is stomach pain, sleepiness or confusion, or fast, deep breathing. The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if ketone levels are high, or if there are symptoms of DKA and the ketone level is not known.

NHS inform says untreated DKA can lead to unconsciousness, so the NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if the warning signs appear.

sections.heading: What are the long-term complications and checks?
sections.body:
Over time, high glucose can damage blood vessels and nerves. The NHS describes complications affecting the eyes, feet and kidneys. In the eyes, damage to blood vessels can cause sight problems (diabetic retinopathy) and, uncommonly, blindness, so adults and children aged 12 or over are offered eye screening every year. In the feet, nerve damage means small cuts may go unnoticed and can become ulcers, so the NHS advises checking the feet every day and having a foot examination at least once a year. In the kidneys, damage usually causes no symptoms at first, so a test is advised every year.

NICE says the annual review for adults includes foot checks and checks for complications such as kidney and nerve problems, and advice about the higher risk of gum disease. NICE says children with type 1 diabetes should have their blood pressure checked every year after they turn 12.

faqs.q: Is type 1 diabetes the same as type 2?
faqs.a: No. Type 1 is an autoimmune condition in which the body makes little or no insulin. Type 2 is a different condition; in the UK about 90% of people diagnosed with diabetes have type 2, according to Diabetes UK.

faqs.q: What are the four Ts of type 1 diabetes?
faqs.a: The NHS lists needing the toilet more, thirst, tiredness and weight loss as the core signs, often remembered as the four Ts. Blurred vision, fruity-smelling breath, slow-healing cuts and frequent infections can also occur.

faqs.q: Why do hypos happen?
faqs.a: Common triggers include taking too much insulin, skipping a meal, vigorous exercise and drinking alcohol on an empty stomach.

faqs.q: Should insulin carry on during illness?
faqs.a: One NHS 111 Wales page says it is very important not to stop treatment when ill. The treatment plan may say whether a temporary increase is needed, and the diabetes care team is the place to ask.

faqs.q: When is diabetic ketoacidosis an emergency?
faqs.a: The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if symptoms are getting worse quickly, or if there is stomach pain, sleepiness or confusion, or fast, deep breathing. DKA is a medical emergency that is treated in hospital.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of ovarian cancer?
sections.body:
The Royal Marsden says symptoms such as bloating usually happen 12 times a month or more, and are new, frequent and persistent. Target Ovarian Cancer also lists feeling full quickly, loss of appetite, pain in the tummy or pelvis, and needing to wee more often or urgently. The Royal Marsden says ovarian cancer often causes vague symptoms, which can make it hard to diagnose.

Cancer Research UK notes that these symptoms are often caused by less serious conditions, such as irritable bowel syndrome.

NHS cancer information describes these symptoms as usually new, frequent and persistent, and recommends seeing a GP about them. A GP appointment is the usual first step, and the GP decides whether tests such as a CA125 blood test are needed.

sections.heading: Who is at risk of ovarian cancer?
sections.body:
The NHS says the risk of ovarian cancer increases with age, and most cases in the UK are in women over 50. The NHS lists an inherited faulty gene, such as the BRCA genes or those linked to Lynch syndrome, a previous breast or bowel cancer, endometriosis, smoking and being overweight among the factors that raise risk.

Cancer Research UK names a fault in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene, and Lynch syndrome, as inherited factors that raise the risk of ovarian cancer. The Royal Marsden says taking the combined contraceptive pill appears to reduce the risk of ovarian cancer. The Royal Marsden says there is no concrete evidence that fertility treatment increases the risk of ovarian cancer.

Risk factors do not guarantee disease.

sections.heading: How are the stage and type of ovarian cancer described?
sections.body:
Ovarian cancer is staged from 1 to 4. Cancer Research UK describes stage 1 as cancer found only in one or both ovaries, and stage 4 as cancer that has spread to distant organs. Grade describes how abnormal the cells look under the microscope. Treatment depends on the type of cancer, where it is, its stage and grade, and the person's general health.

 Target Ovarian Cancer says PARP inhibitors are used for high-grade serous cancer, and the MEK inhibitor trametinib for low-grade serous cancer that has returned or kept growing after platinum chemotherapy.

MedlinePlus says ovarian cancer is seldom found early, and that survival is high when it is found and treated before it has spread beyond the ovary.

sections.heading: How is ovarian cancer treated?
sections.body:
The main treatments are surgery and chemotherapy. Surgery is usually the first step. In stage 1 ovarian cancer, surgery is the main treatment, and some people also have chemotherapy. The NHS says chemotherapy is usually given in addition to surgery, and is sometimes given before surgery to shrink the cancer. Radiotherapy is rarely used for ovarian cancer, and is sometimes used to reduce symptoms.

Target Ovarian Cancer describes targeted treatments. Target Ovarian Cancer says PARP inhibitors are generally offered for stage 3 or 4 high-grade serous cancer that has responded to platinum-based chemotherapy, and can usually only be used once. Target Ovarian Cancer says bevacizumab can be given with the PARP inhibitor olaparib as a maintenance treatment for newly diagnosed disease.

sections.heading: Life after treatment for ovarian cancer
sections.body:
NHS inform says that anyone who has not yet been through the menopause will usually be brought into it by treatment. Cancer and its treatment can cause physical and emotional changes that affect a person's sex life, and difficulties usually slowly improve after treatment.

Follow-up involves regular check-ups. CA125 blood tests are sometimes done as part of follow-up, and a rising level may be a sign that the cancer has returned. NHS inform says people do not have to wait for a follow-up appointment if they have concerns about symptoms.

faqs.q: How is ovarian cancer diagnosed?
faqs.a: A blood test and a scan are usually the first tests. CA125 is a blood marker that is not always raised in ovarian cancer and can also be raised by other conditions, and imaging may be an ultrasound, CT or MRI scan. Tissue from a biopsy or from surgery is examined under a microscope to confirm the diagnosis.

faqs.q: Do bloating and tummy pain mean ovarian cancer?
faqs.a: Not usually. Cancer Research UK notes that these symptoms are often caused by less serious conditions, such as irritable bowel syndrome. NHS cancer information describes these symptoms as usually new, frequent and persistent, and recommends seeing a GP about them.

faqs.q: Will treatment bring on the menopause?
faqs.a: NHS inform says that if the person has not already been through the menopause, treatment will usually cause it.

faqs.q: What are PARP inhibitors?
faqs.a: They are targeted drugs. Target Ovarian Cancer says PARP inhibitors are generally offered for stage 3 or 4 high-grade serous cancer that has responded to platinum-based chemotherapy, and can usually only be used once.

faqs.q: Can ovarian cancer come back?
faqs.a: Yes. Target Ovarian Cancer says follow-up appointments are used to check for any return of the cancer, as well as how treatment has affected daily life. A person who has concerns after treatment does not have to wait for a follow-up appointment before getting in touch with their care team.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of cervical cancer?
sections.body:
The NHS lists unusual vaginal bleeding, including bleeding after sex or between periods, as a symptom of cervical cancer. Other symptoms are changes in vaginal discharge, pain during sex, and pelvic or lower back pain.

Early cervical cancer often causes no symptoms, so the NHS says that symptoms appearing between regular screening appointments should not wait for the next one. A GP appointment is the route to getting symptoms checked, rather than waiting for the next screening appointment.

These symptoms can have other causes, so they do not by themselves mean cancer.

sections.heading: What causes cervical cancer?
sections.body:
The NHS says nearly all cervical cancers are linked to infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV).

 All children aged 12 to 13 are offered the HPV vaccine, and everyone with a cervix aged 25 to 64 is invited for regular cervical screening. This includes women and anyone else who has a cervix. Screening looks for HPV and abnormal cells before cancer develops.

 Cervical screening is not a test for cancer.

sections.heading: How is cervical cancer diagnosed?
sections.body:
Diagnosis often begins with an abnormal screening result. Colposcopy is usually offered after an abnormal screening result: the cervix is looked at closely through a magnifying instrument, and a small tissue sample (biopsy) may be taken from anywhere that looks unusual. A loop excision (LLETZ) or cone biopsy can also give tissue to examine. Colposcopy does not establish a diagnosis of cancer on its own. A biopsy does.

Most findings at colposcopy are cell changes that are not cancer, and the NHS says cancer is found only in rare cases.

If cancer is found, tests such as an MRI scan, a PET-CT scan or a chest X-ray may be used to see how far it has spread. Doctors describe this as the stage, using the FIGO system, which has four stages numbered 1 to 4 based on the size of the cancer and whether it has spread.

sections.heading: How is cervical cancer treated?
sections.body:
Treatment usually includes surgery, chemotherapy or radiotherapy, and depends on the size and type of the cancer and where it is. Surgery is the main treatment for early disease, and the types include LLETZ, cone biopsy, hysterectomy and trachelectomy. Radiotherapy is mainly used for more advanced cancer or when surgery is not suitable, and chemotherapy or radiotherapy may be given after surgery.

Cancer Research UK says chemotherapy can be given at the same time as radiotherapy, called chemoradiotherapy, for stage 1B2 to stage 4A cervical cancer, and that cisplatin is the most common drug. For stage 2B, chemoradiotherapy is the most likely treatment, and for some larger stage 2A cancers it may be suggested instead of surgery. In stage 4A a few people may be offered a pelvic exenteration, a major operation.

For cervical cancer that is persistent, has come back or has spread, NICE recommends the immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab with chemotherapy, with or without the targeted drug bevacizumab, for some adults. Small cell cancer of the cervix is rare and is treated differently.

sections.heading: Fertility and support
sections.body:
People are usually referred to a fertility specialist before treatment starts, so that options such as storing eggs, embryos or ovarian tissue can be discussed. Options such as storing eggs or embryos before treatment can be discussed. Trachelectomy is one operation designed for people who wish to keep the option of pregnancy.

 Outlook is generally better when cervical cancer is found before it has spread outside the cervix, which is one reason early diagnosis matters.

faqs.q: Does an abnormal screening result mean cancer?
faqs.a: No. An abnormal result leads to colposcopy, a closer look at the cervix. Most findings at colposcopy are cell changes that are not cancer, and the NHS says cancer is found only in rare cases. Most abnormal findings at colposcopy are cell changes rather than cancer.

faqs.q: What happens at colposcopy?
faqs.a: The cervix is looked at closely, and a small tissue sample (biopsy) may be taken from anywhere that looks unusual. Tissue can also be taken with a loop excision (LLETZ) or cone biopsy. Colposcopy is usually the first step after an abnormal screening result.

faqs.q: Does bleeding after sex mean cervical cancer?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. These symptoms can have other causes, so they do not by themselves mean cancer. The NHS advises that symptoms between screening appointments should not wait for the next appointment, and that a GP can check them.

faqs.q: Can I still have children after treatment?
faqs.a: It depends on the treatment. People are usually referred to a fertility specialist before treatment starts, so that options such as storing eggs, embryos or ovarian tissue can be discussed. Egg or embryo storage before treatment can be discussed, and for some people with early cancer a trachelectomy can remove the cancer while keeping the womb.

faqs.q: Who is invited for cervical screening?
faqs.a: The NHS says everyone with a cervix aged 25 to 64 is invited for regular screening. All children aged 12 to 13 are offered the HPV vaccine.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of PCOS?
sections.body:
Irregular or infrequent periods, extra hair on the face or body (hirsutism) and difficulty getting pregnant are among the most commonly listed signs. Acne, oily skin, weight gain, particularly around the waist, and thinning scalp hair also appear on some lists.

NHS leaflets say women with PCOS may ovulate infrequently or not at all, which can make it harder to get pregnant. An NHS hospital leaflet says depression and mood swings can also occur.

Symptoms vary a lot. NHS hospital leaflets say some women have mild symptoms, while others are affected more severely by a wider range of symptoms. NHS inform now titles its page on the condition polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) and describes it as previously known as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).

sections.heading: How is PCOS diagnosed?
sections.body:
Diagnosis commonly uses the Rotterdam criteria: at least two of three features (irregular or absent periods, signs of raised male hormones, and polycystic-looking ovaries on a scan), after other causes have been ruled out. A scan is not always needed: when irregular periods and signs of raised male hormones are both present, an ultrasound is not necessary for diagnosis.

A leaflet from an NHS trust says polycystic ovaries on their own do not need treatment. One NHS leaflet says up to 1 in 4 young women have polycystic-looking ovaries on a scan, and another NHS trust leaflet says polycystic ovaries by themselves do not need treatment.

 A 2025 all-party parliamentary group inquiry into PCOS reported significant gaps in diagnosis, treatment and long-term support.

sections.heading: How is PCOS treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says there is no cure for PCOS, but the symptoms can be treated. NHS leaflets say losing weight can help people who are overweight, with more regular periods and less acne and excess hair over time.

NHS leaflets say the combined contraceptive pill can be used to regulate periods and ease symptoms driven by male hormones, and that metformin is sometimes used off-label. Fertility medicines are available, and cosmetic hair treatments are also used for excess hair growth.

sections.heading: PCOS and fertility
sections.body:
PCOS can disrupt ovulation, which can make it harder to conceive.

NHS information says medicines such as clomifene can be used to trigger ovulation in women who are trying to conceive. If medicines do not work, in vitro fertilisation (IVF) may be offered, and a simple surgical procedure called laparoscopic ovarian drilling may be recommended. The NHS says that with treatment, most women with PCOS are able to get pregnant.

An NHS trust page says PCOS is one of the recognised causes of gestational diabetes, which can lead to pre-eclampsia.

sections.heading: PCOS, long-term health and mood
sections.body:
UK sources list type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, sleep apnoea and a raised risk of cancer of the womb lining among the possible long-term health risks. Infrequent or absent periods are a risk factor for thickening of the womb lining.

 The 2025 all-party parliamentary group report says psychological support is rarely offered despite well-established mental health risks, and recommends better recognition of and support for mental wellbeing.

faqs.q: Can I get pregnant with PCOS?
faqs.a: Most women with PCOS are able to get pregnant with treatment. The NHS says that with treatment most women with PCOS are able to get pregnant. PCOS can disrupt ovulation, which can make it harder to conceive. Medicines such as clomifene can be used to trigger ovulation, and IVF may be offered if medicines do not work.

faqs.q: Does having polycystic ovaries on a scan mean I have PCOS?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Polycystic-looking ovaries are common on a scan, and an NHS trust leaflet says they do not need treatment by themselves. One NHS leaflet says up to 1 in 4 young women have polycystic-looking ovaries on a scan, and polycystic ovaries by themselves do not need treatment. Diagnosis commonly needs at least two of three features, after other causes have been ruled out.

faqs.q: Is there a cure for PCOS?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no cure, but the symptoms can be treated. Losing weight can help people who are overweight, the combined contraceptive pill can be used to regulate periods, and fertility treatment is available.

faqs.q: Does PCOS raise the risk of type 2 diabetes?
faqs.a: UK sources list type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, sleep apnoea and a raised risk of cancer of the womb lining among the possible long-term health risks.

faqs.q: Can PCOS affect mental health?
faqs.a: The 2025 all-party parliamentary group report says psychological support is rarely offered despite well-established mental health risks, and recommends better recognition of and support for mental wellbeing.
